title: When Fire Drills Happen Every Day
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that recurring 'all hands on deck' crunches are a symptom of poor leadership planning, not unavoidable business reality. Occasional emergencies happen even to well-run teams, but a pattern of frequent last-minute scrambles signals disorganization at the top, and it burns out and demoralizes the people asked to absorb the churn. The piece connects chronic fire drills to leaders who don't prioritize, don't set advance deadlines, or chase perfectionism past the point of usefulness. It closes by framing preparation time as a form of respect: leaders who protect their team's runway to plan are treating people's time as valuable, while leaders who don't are implicitly signaling disrespect.
points: Occasional emergencies are normal, but frequent fire drills reflect a leadership failure to plan.
Chronic last-minute scrambling demoralizes teams and drives burnout.
Setting advance deadlines and checking in early prevents most fire drills before they happen.
A fire-drill culture often coexists with leaders who treat colleagues as disposable resources.
Giving teams adequate lead time to plan is framed as a core sign of respect from a leader.
quotes: The continual thrash created by last-minute work and the rush to complete tasks and projects demoralizes a team
Fire drills reflect a leader’s inability to manage the work of others.
The best leaders set advanced deadlines where review can occur well ahead of the need to rush
A fire drill mentality is most common in organizational cultures where leaders are unconcerned about the well-being
There is no excuse for ongoing fire drills on any team or in any organization.
When leaders don’t plan for them, deadlines become a sign of disrespect.
